Q: How can I get vscode recent file/folder/workspaces on linux with cli tools or via code? A:

VS Code stores recent workspaces in ~/.config/Code/User/globalStorage/state.vscdb — but are you using stock VS Code, VSCodium, Code - OSS, or something like Cursor? The DB path differs per fork, and if you're on VSCodium the key name inside the DB may differ too. Knowing this upfront avoids you running a script that silently queries the wrong file.

Q: Handling of Negative Exponent in Recursion, Confused A:

The code has two return statements in a row; the second one will never be reached. The first one belongs inside the brackets after if(exp < 0). Further, that return statement will always return either 0 or 1, because it's doing integer arithmetic. Casting the result to double doesn't change the calculation itself. But that doesn't matter; power returns int, so it can't handle negative exponents sensibly.

Q: How to prevent re-processing when reading pending entries (ID 0) in Redis stream using XREADGROUP? A:

When using CLAIM min-idle-time, the value should be set according to the duration it takes your consumers to process messages. For example, if messages are [almost] always processed in 1000 milliseconds, you can set min-idle-time to 1100. Hence, if a message was not ACKed during this time - then something most likely went wrong on the consumer side, and other consumers should handle it.

Using XPENDING you can see who is the current owner of a specific message, the number of milliseconds that elapsed since the last time this message was delivered to that consumer, and also the message's deliveries counter.

Q: What is unicode character 2028 (LS / Line Separator) used for? A:

As answer to forward thinking @Elijah I would highly discourage to use 0x2028 / LS / Line Separator, and go git way: use only /n and don't give a damn about Windows, or let those magic happen with the file on Windows computer with replacement to /r/n

As of 2025, shift+Enter enters 0x2028 / LS / Line Separator) in following software:

  • macOS Notes (and most likely iOS, padOS, consistently in all Apple OS products)
  • Apple Pages (tip how show hidden characters)
  • LibreOffice

But NOT in :

  • Sublime Text Editor
    It for shift+Enter enters usual line break, that is treated as
    Paragraph break ¶ (Pilcrow sign) in Notes, Pages, LibreOffice

(Please add comment or extend what happens on Windows... Notepad, MS Office, Notepad++)

The problems begin when copy-pasting text (oh, gosh!) between apps:

  1. Between Notes and Pages no problem, naturally
  2. From anything to LibreOffice, all 0x2028 are silently removed
  3. From LibreOffice - LibreOffice replaces 0x2028 / LS / Line Separator with /n
  4. From Notes into Sublime Text Editor
    not supported, so line breaks disappear (but at least it by default renders it as <0x2028>; still possible to select, copy and paste)
  5. From Notes to VS Code
    It disapproves, suggest to remove and fails to render:
    rendered as question mark in rombus, i.e. U+FFFD � REPLACEMENT CHARACTER
    aka "garbage in file".

Exact versions:

  • Notes macOS 15.4.1 (24E263)
  • Pages 13.1
  • Sublime Text Editor Build 4200
  • LibreOffice 25.2.5.2
  • VS Code 1.102.0

And to all folks let us pray/vote/raise awareness that it would be solved nice and for all by 2028
as it is 0x2028 clearly !

Q: Best CPUs for Numpy A:

If your code is actually representative of your application, and you want to speed it up, I think it would be better to try rewriting it to use multiple cores/threads so you can see how it performs on different CPU types. I chose numexpr because it does multi-threading and JIT for you - extremely simply.

Here is the port - you can just tack it onto the end of your own setup code:

import numexpr as ne

# Choose number of threads to use
ne.set_num_threads(nthreads=2)

ne.evaluate('X>Y')

For comparison purposes, your original code runs in 47ms on my machine.

Depending on the number of threads I select, I get the following times:

N threads Time (ms)
1 66
2 35
4 20
8 11
16 9.9
32 9.8

Hopefully you can see that just 2 cores/threads beats single-threaded calculation by some margin and it scales out pretty well to 8+ threads, so it is possible to benefit from multi-core CPUs.
